title: A Delhi Hotel Was Licensed for Six Rooms. It Was Running Twenty-Five. Twenty-Two People Are Dead.
excerpt: The Malviya Nagar fire has killed 22 people, including 13 foreign nationals, and exposed a fire safety crisis in the capital's unregulated hospitality sector
body:
The fire started in the early hours of Wednesday, June 3, at the Flourish Stay Bed and Breakfast in Hauz Rani, a congested pocket of South Delhi's Malviya Nagar. By the time the Delhi Fire Service brought it under control, 21 people had been declared dead at nearby hospitals. On Saturday night, a 22nd victim — a Nigerian national named Okale, who had been on ventilator support at Safdarjung Hospital — succumbed to his burn injuries.

Twenty-two dead. Thirteen of them foreign nationals, from Kyrgyzstan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Iraq, Congo, Mozambique, and Liberia. One of them a sixteen-year-old girl.

This is now one of the deadliest fire tragedies in Delhi's recent history. And the details that have emerged since paint a picture of systemic failure, regulatory negligence, and a hospitality sector operating well beyond the bounds of safety and legality.

Sealed Windows, Locked Basement

When investigators entered the charred remains of the Flourish Stay building, what they found was damning. The windows and glass panels of the structure had been completely sealed — leaving no outlet for smoke to escape. The entrance to the basement was locked from the inside. Rescue teams took nearly ten minutes just to gain access to the basement level, from which six to seven people were eventually pulled out alive.

The hotel was licensed under Delhi's Bed and Breakfast scheme to operate six rooms. It was running twenty-five.

Delhi Fire Service officials rescued more than 40 people from the burning building. Many were pulled from upper floors and the basement in the hours after the fire broke out. Fifteen injured individuals were admitted to Max Hospital in Saket, with nine more in the intensive care unit. The hospital reported that "all ventilated patients are stable and showing signs of improvement," but the damage — physical, psychological, and institutional — is already done.

Arrests and an Expanding Probe

Delhi Police moved quickly. Hotel owner Lovkesh Bajaj was arrested and remanded to four days of police custody. Cook Keshav Negi, whose alleged negligence investigators say triggered the blaze — reportedly through a cooking gas leak — was arrested separately and brought to the incident site on Sunday to reconstruct the sequence of events.

Two other individuals, Sweety Sarkar and Pushpo Sarkar, have also been arrested. Police have filed an FIR under charges of culpable homicide and continue to widen the investigation, questioning multiple people associated with the hotel.

But the arrests have raised as many questions as they have answered. Bajaj, it has emerged, was previously arrested for allegedly helping undocumented Bangladeshi nationals obtain forged identity documents. The hotel's history of operating far beyond its licensed capacity was evidently known, or at least knowable, to authorities long before the fire.

A Systemic Problem

The Malviya Nagar fire is not an isolated tragedy. It sits within a pattern of fatal fires in Delhi's informal and semi-regulated commercial spaces — a pattern driven by unchecked construction, inadequate fire safety inspections, and a licensing regime that exists on paper but rarely in practice.

In response, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi announced plans to cancel the licenses of 12 hotels and seal 20 others. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta has sought an official report. The Ministry of External Affairs is coordinating with embassies whose nationals were killed or injured.

These are reactive measures. The question for Delhi — a city where thousands of budget hotels, guest houses, and bed-and-breakfast establishments operate in congested residential areas with minimal oversight — is whether there will be preventive ones.

For the Diaspora, a Familiar Horror

For Indians living abroad, the Malviya Nagar fire is a reminder of a risk that sits at the intersection of infrastructure and governance. NRIs returning to India for visits or business routinely book budget accommodations in South Delhi. Many of those establishments operate under the same Bed and Breakfast licensing scheme that Flourish Stay allegedly exploited.

The fire also carries an international dimension that the Indian government cannot ignore. Thirteen foreign nationals — students, travellers, migrant workers — died in a building that should not have been operating as a hotel at its scale. The diplomatic fallout is already in motion. Embassy officials from multiple countries are in contact with Delhi authorities.

For the 22 people who checked into the Flourish Stay and did not check out, the fire safety infrastructure of one of the world's largest capitals failed catastrophically. Whether it will change is an open question. The precedents are not encouraging.
